title: Isolation-based Spherical Ensemble Representations for Tabular Anomaly Detection
summary: Unsupervised tabular anomaly detection still faces conflicting distributional assumptions, computational inefficiency, and difficulty handling diverse anomaly types (global, local, dependency). ISER builds t independent hypersphere partitionings from random ψ-point subsets whose radii (nearest-neighbor distances within the subset) serve as a monotonic transformation of local density, encodes each point as a vector Φ(x)∈R^t with φ=1−1/r when covered by a hypersphere and φ=1 otherwise, and scores points by the mean of Φ (ISER-A), by cosine similarity to an all-ones anomaly reference vector (ISER-S), or by running Isolation Forest on the Φ-space with an inverted path-length score (ISER-IF). On 20 real-world datasets ISER-S achieves the best average AUC-ROC of 0.8523 among 14 methods, and ISER-IF lifts iForest on Ionosphere from 0.8530 to 0.9314 AUC-ROC.

match_target.why: The user hint explicitly names Table IV, ISER-IF on Ionosphere. It is the headline number of contribution 3 (ISER boosting iForest, 0.8530 -> 0.9314) rather than a side ablation, and it exercises the full pipeline end-to-end — hypersphere partitioning, ensemble representations, iForest on the Φ-space, and the inverted scoring function — on a tiny 351x32 dataset, so the whole ψ grid x 5 repeats runs in CPU minutes.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: the paper reports no std (only the mean of 5 runs, so rule 1 cannot apply), and Ionosphere has 351 points, below rule 2's 2,000-example threshold; the metric is a bounded AUC-ROC printed in [0,1], so the band is 0.02 absolute.

requirements.stmt: For each of the t partitionings, sample a subset Di of exactly ψ points from D without replacement; each partitioning uses a different random subset.
requirements.quote: we begin by randomly sampling a subset Di ⊂D of size ψ without replacement

requirements.stmt: Each sampled point z becomes a hypersphere center whose radius r[z] equals the distance to its nearest neighbor within Di \ {z}.
requirements.cite: Sec. III-A, Eq. for r[z]; Algorithm 1, line 5
requirements.quote: The radius of this hypersphere is determined by the distance between z and its nearest neighbor in Di \ {z}

requirements.stmt: For a point x, build the covering set Ci(x) = {z in Di : ||x−z|| ≤ r[z]} and select the covering hypersphere with the smallest radius as ẑi(x).
requirements.quote: we select the covering hypersphere with the smallest radius

requirements.stmt: Representation value: φi(x) = 1 − 1/r[ẑi(x)] when Ci(x) is non-empty; φi(x) = 1 when x is covered by no hypersphere in Hi (Eq. 1).
requirements.quote: When x is covered by no hypersphere in Hi, we assign φi(x) = 1

requirements.stmt: Concatenate the per-partitioning values into the ensemble representation Φ(x) = [φ1(x), ..., φt(x)] ∈ R^t.
requirements.quote: The ensemble representation of point x is constructed by concatenating the coverage indicators from all t partitionings

requirements.stmt: ISER-A score: arithmetic mean of the t components of Φ(x), bounded above by 1.
requirements.quote: The average-based anomaly score is computed as the arithmetic mean of all ensemble components

requirements.stmt: ISER-S score: cosine similarity between Φ(x) and the all-ones anomaly reference vector 1 = [1,...,1] ∈ R^t.
requirements.quote: The similarity-based approach begins by defining an ideal anomaly reference pattern that represents the theoretical behavior of a perfect anomaly.

requirements.stmt: ISER-IF: train iForest on the transformed space {Φ(x)} and invert the scoring so longer path lengths mean more anomalous: S_ISER-IF(x,n) = 1 − 2^(−E(h(Φ(x)))/c(n)), because anomalies cluster tightly in Φ-space while normal points scatter.

requirements.stmt: Hyperparameters: ψ searched over {2^m, m=1,...,8} = {2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256} and t = 200 by default, for iForest, iNNE, IDK, ADERH and the proposed methods.
requirements.quote: For iForest, iNNE, IDK, ADERH and proposed methods, ψ ∈{2m, m = 1, 2, . . . , 8} and with default t = 200.

requirements.stmt: Evaluation metric is AUC-ROC; each experiment is repeated 5 times and the average is reported.
requirements.quote: We use Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC) as evaluation metrics.

requirements.stmt: Fully unsupervised protocol: train on the entire contaminated dataset (no clean normal training set) and evaluate on the same data; identical protocol for all methods.
requirements.quote: All methods are evaluated on the same contaminated datasets to ensure fair comparison.
